topics.description: How large-scale software systems are actually built: the path a request takes, how load is spread, where data lives and how it is copied, what consistency really costs, and how systems keep working when parts of them fail. The through-line is tradeoffs — every technique here buys something and charges for it, and the goal is to be able to name both sides.

subtopics.title: The path of a request, from DNS to disk
subtopics.description: Trace a single HTTP request end to end and name every hop it makes: DNS resolution, TLS termination, CDN or edge, load balancer, application server, cache, database, and back. Teach that 'the system' is this path, that every box on it is a place where latency is added and failure can originate, and that most design conversations are really arguments about which hop should absorb which work. Cover why the numbers matter — memory access vs SSD vs cross-region round trip differ by orders of magnitude, so where a piece of data lives dominates how fast a request can possibly be. Also cover the difference between latency and throughput, why averages hide the users who are actually suffering (p50 vs p99 tail latency), and how a fan-out request inherits the tail of its slowest dependency. This is the mental scaffolding every later subtopic hangs on, so keep each card grounded in the concrete hop it is about rather than abstract principle.

cards.title: A request's latency is the sum of every hop it takes
cards.summary: There is no such thing as making 'the system' faster in the abstract — only a specific hop.
cards.body:
When a client hits your site, the request does not travel as one thing — it passes through DNS resolution, TLS handshake, maybe a CDN, a load balancer, an application server, a cache, and a database, then back the same way. End-to-end latency is the **sum** of the time spent at each hop, not some property of the system as a whole.

This is why 'make it faster' is not an engineering task until you know which hop dominates. If the database is 80ms of a 100ms response, shaving 10ms off the application code is close to invisible to the user.

Every later technique — caching, replication, CDNs, connection pooling — is really a move that **relocates work between hops** on this chain. Caching moves work from the database hop to a faster hop closer to the client. Replication moves read work off a single overloaded hop onto several. Understanding the chain is the prerequisite for understanding why any of those techniques help.

cards.title: A request's total time is set by its slowest parallel branch
cards.summary: Fan-out doesn't average latency across dependencies — it inherits the worst one.
cards.body:
```diagram
app server --> service A (20ms)
           --> service B (15ms)
           --> service C (300ms, degraded)
           --> wait for all three --> respond
```

Many real requests aren't a straight line — they fan out to several dependencies in parallel and wait for all of them before responding. The naive intuition is that parallelizing three calls costs about as much as the slowest one alone, which is true **when everything is healthy**. The problem is that it also means the response time is only ever as good as the worst-behaving dependency at that moment.

This is why a single degraded, non-critical dependency can drag down an otherwise fast page. It's also why timeouts on fan-out calls matter more than on simple sequential ones — one slow branch without a timeout can hold the whole response hostage.

cards.title: Average latency hides the users who are actually suffering
cards.summary: The mean tells you almost nothing about what any individual request felt like.
cards.body:
❌ **Average latency tells you how the site feels** - a dashboard showing '45ms average' looks healthy, so it's tempting to treat it as the metric that matters.

✅ **Tail latency (p99, p999) is what real users experience** - if 1% of requests take 3 seconds, that's not a rounding error at scale: at 10,000 requests per second, 100 requests every second are having a bad time. Averages get pulled toward the bulk of fast requests and quietly bury the slow tail. p50 tells you the median experience; p99 tells you what your worst-served users are living through, and at scale that's not a small population — it's thousands of people per hour.

cards.title: DNS is a cache with a TTL you don't control end to end
cards.summary: Resolving a hostname to an IP is itself a multi-hop lookup with its own staleness window.
cards.body:
Before a browser can even open a connection, it has to resolve a hostname to an IP address, and that resolution is itself a small distributed system: a recursive resolver (often your ISP's or a public one like 1.1.1.1) walks from root servers to TLD servers to your domain's authoritative nameserver, caching the answer along the way according to a TTL you set in your DNS records.

That TTL is a real design lever. A short TTL (seconds to minutes) lets you redirect traffic quickly — useful for failover — but means every client re-resolves more often, adding latency and load on your nameservers. A long TTL is cheap and fast but means a DNS change can take hours to fully propagate, because resolvers you don't control are still serving the old answer from cache.

cards.title: Latency and throughput are different numbers and can move in opposite directions
cards.summary: How fast one request finishes and how many requests finish per second are not the same measurement.
cards.body:
**Latency** is how long a single request takes, start to finish. **Throughput** is how many requests the system completes per unit of time. It's tempting to treat these as the same thing scaled differently, but they diverge in important ways.

Batching is the clearest example: grouping ten writes into one database transaction can *increase* throughput (more total writes per second) while *increasing* the latency of any individual write, because it now waits for nine others to be ready. Conversely, adding more concurrent workers can raise throughput without changing per-request latency at all, as long as the system isn't yet saturated.

A design that optimizes purely for throughput can quietly make the experience worse for any one user, and a design obsessed with minimizing latency for a single request can leave capacity on the table. Both numbers need to be stated explicitly, because 'faster' is ambiguous between them.

cards.title: The request path is a chain, and every link can fail on its own
cards.summary: Draw the hops and you have also drawn the list of things that can independently break.
cards.body:
```diagram
client --> DNS --> CDN / edge --> load balancer --> app server --> cache --> database
                                                                        |
                                                                        +--> (miss) database
```

Each arrow in that chain is a network hop with its own latency, and each box is a component with its own failure mode. DNS can return a stale record. TLS can fail to negotiate. The CDN can serve a stale asset. The load balancer can route to a dead server. The app server can throw. The cache can be cold. The database can be slow.

The reason system design conversations spend so much time on this chain is that it is a literal inventory: every box is a place latency gets added, and every box is a place failure can originate. You cannot reason about reliability or performance without first being able to name the hops.

cards.title: TLS termination decides who pays the encryption cost, and where
cards.summary: Someone has to do the handshake — the question is which box.
cards.body:
Before any application data flows, the client and server perform a TLS handshake: negotiating a cipher, exchanging keys, and establishing an encrypted channel. This costs extra round trips (though modern TLS 1.3 and session resumption shrink it considerably) and real CPU for the cryptographic operations.

Where that handshake is **terminated** — decrypted — is a design choice. Terminating at a CDN or load balancer means the expensive part happens close to the user and once, with the rest of the internal hops potentially running over a trusted private network unencrypted or with cheaper re-encryption. Terminating deep inside your infrastructure, at each app server, means every hop pays the cost redundantly but nothing in between is ever in plaintext. Neither is universally correct — it's a tradeoff between performance and defense-in-depth.

cards.title: Where data lives determines how fast it can possibly be fetched
cards.summary: No amount of clever code beats the physical distance to the data.
cards.body:
The orders of magnitude between storage layers aren't a rounding error — they're the whole game:

- L1/L2 CPU cache: under 1 nanosecond to a few nanoseconds
- Main memory (RAM): roughly 100 nanoseconds
- SSD random read: roughly 100 microseconds — about 1,000x slower than RAM
- Same-datacenter network round trip: roughly 0.5 millisecond
- Cross-region round trip (e.g. US to Europe): roughly 100 milliseconds — another 100-200x on top of that

A request that could be answered from memory and one that requires a cross-region round trip differ by roughly six orders of magnitude. This is why 'where does this data live' is one of the first questions in any design: it sets a hard floor on how fast a request can possibly be, independent of how well the code around it is written.

subtopics.title: Scaling up, scaling out, and why servers must forget
subtopics.description: Vertical scaling (a bigger machine) versus horizontal scaling (more machines), and why the second one requires a design change rather than just a purchase order. The central idea is statelessness: if any app server can serve any request, you can add and remove servers freely, and the load balancer's job stays trivial. Cover what breaks that property — in-memory sessions, local file uploads, in-process caches, background timers running on every replica — and where that state has to move instead (shared session store, object storage, distributed cache). Cover the load balancer itself: round robin vs least-connections, health checks and how a failing server is removed from rotation, and why sticky sessions are a compromise that reintroduces the problem statelessness solved. Close on the honest counterpoint that vertical scaling is underrated for small systems and buys real time.

cards.title: Statelessness is what makes horizontal scaling possible
cards.summary: Adding a server only helps if that server can answer any request equally well.
cards.body:
**Vertical scaling** means buying a bigger machine — more CPU, more RAM. It's simple, requires no architectural change, and for a lot of systems it's genuinely the right first move. **Horizontal scaling** means adding more machines of the same size, and it is not just a bigger purchase order — it requires a real design property first: **statelessness**.

An app server is stateless when any instance can serve any incoming request with identical correctness, because it holds nothing in memory that only it knows. If that's true, a load balancer can send a request to whichever server is free, and you can add or remove servers at will without anything breaking.

The moment a server holds something only it has — a session in memory, a file just uploaded to local disk, an in-process cache — that server is no longer interchangeable. Requests that depend on that state now have to find *that specific server again*, and the load balancer's simple job (send it anywhere healthy) gets complicated. Every piece of state trapped in a single process is a hidden ceiling on how far horizontal scaling can actually take you.

cards.title: A health check is how a load balancer learns a server is lying
cards.summary: Being 'up' and being 'able to serve requests correctly' are not the same claim.

cards.title: A readiness probe decides when a server is allowed to receive traffic
cards.summary: Being alive and being ready are separate questions Kubernetes asks separately.
cards.body:
```yaml
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
```

A **liveness** probe asks 'should this process be restarted' — is it deadlocked or crashed. A **readiness** probe asks a different question: 'should traffic be routed here right now.' A server can be perfectly alive but not ready — still warming up a cache, still connecting to the database, or deliberately unready during a graceful shutdown while it drains in-flight requests.

Getting this distinction wrong is a common source of self-inflicted outages: routing traffic to a server the moment it starts, before its dependencies are actually connected, produces a wave of errors that a correctly configured readiness probe would have avoided entirely by holding it out of rotation for those first few seconds.

cards.title: Round robin and least-connections answer different questions
cards.summary: How a load balancer picks the next server matters more once requests aren't all the same size.
cards.body:
**Round robin** sends each new request to the next server in a rotating list, regardless of what those servers are currently doing. It's simple and works fine when requests are roughly uniform in cost.

**Least-connections** sends each new request to whichever server currently has the fewest active connections. This matters once request cost varies — a server stuck handling a few slow, expensive requests won't keep getting piled on with new ones just because it's 'next in line.'

Neither strategy fixes an underlying capacity problem; they just distribute load more or less intelligently across the capacity you have. Least-connections is generally the safer default once request durations vary meaningfully, which in practice is almost always.

cards.title: State has to move somewhere — it doesn't just disappear
cards.summary: Making app servers stateless means giving that state a new, shared home.
cards.body:
```diagram
                 +--> app server 1 (stateless) --+
load balancer -->+--> app server 2 (stateless) --+--> shared session store (Redis)
                 +--> app server 3 (stateless) --+--> object storage (uploads)
```

Statelessness doesn't mean the state ceases to exist — it means it moves out of any single server's process into something all the servers can reach equally. Session data goes into a shared store like Redis or a database instead of an in-memory dictionary. Uploaded files go to object storage (S3-style) instead of local disk. A cache that used to live in-process becomes a shared cache like Memcached.

Once that move happens, every app server in the diagram is truly interchangeable: the load balancer can route anywhere, any server can be killed and replaced, and scaling out is just adding more identical boxes to the left side of the diagram.

cards.title: Sticky sessions reintroduce the problem statelessness was meant to solve
cards.summary: Pinning a user to a server is a workaround, not a fix, and it comes with a real cost.
cards.body:
A **sticky session** configures the load balancer to route a given user's requests to the same backend server every time, usually via a cookie. It's often reached for as a quick fix when session state lives in a server's local memory and moving it to a shared store feels like more work than it's worth.

The compromise is real: that server is no longer interchangeable for that user. If it goes down, that user's session is gone. If that server gets overloaded, you can't shift its stuck-to-it users elsewhere without disrupting them. Autoscaling and rolling deploys get harder because removing a server now has a user-visible cost it wouldn't otherwise have.

Sticky sessions aren't always wrong — sometimes they're a pragmatic stopgap — but they should be understood as *reintroducing* the coupling between a user and a specific server that a shared session store would have removed entirely.

cards.title: Vertical scaling is underrated for a system that isn't big yet
cards.summary: A bigger machine buys real time and costs zero architectural complexity.
cards.body:
It's easy to treat horizontal scaling as the mature, 'real' answer and vertical scaling as a stopgap for beginners. For a lot of systems that's backwards. A modern single machine can have dozens of cores, hundreds of gigabytes of RAM, and fast local NVMe storage — enough to serve a surprising amount of real-world traffic without a single distributed-systems concern.

Vertical scaling has a real ceiling (you eventually run out of bigger machines to buy, and a single box is a single point of failure), but until you're near that ceiling, it buys the same relief as horizontal scaling with none of the cost: no statelessness requirement, no load balancer, no shared session store, no consistency questions between replicas.

The honest framing is that vertical scaling delays the day you need to solve the harder problem, and for many systems that day never actually needs to come.

cards.title: 'We'll just add more servers' assumes a property you may not have
cards.summary: Scaling out a stateful app doesn't just fail to help — it can make things actively wrong.
cards.body:
❌ **We'll just add more servers if we need more capacity** - it sounds like a purely operational lever, something you turn up when traffic grows, independent of how the code is written.

✅ **Adding servers only helps if any server can handle any request** - if your app keeps session data, uploaded files, or per-user caches in local memory or local disk, adding a second server doesn't double capacity — it means roughly half of users start hitting a server that has never seen them before. Best case, that's a cache miss and a slower response. Worse case, it's a logged-out user, a missing upload, or a request that fails outright. Scaling out a stateful system doesn't just underperform — it can turn a working single-server app into a broken multi-server one.

subtopics.title: Caching and the arithmetic of hit rates
subtopics.description: A cache is a bet that the same data will be asked for again soon, and the payoff is computable: effective latency is hit_rate * fast_path + (1 - hit_rate) * slow_path, which is why a 90% hit rate is far less than twice as good as 80%. Teach the layers a cached value can live in — browser, CDN, application-level (Redis/Memcached), and the database's own buffer pool — and that each layer caches a different shape of thing. Cover the read patterns (cache-aside as the default, read-through, write-through vs write-behind) and what each does on a miss. Cover expiry honestly: TTLs are a bet on staleness tolerance, explicit invalidation is correct but hard, and the two failure modes worth naming early are the thundering herd when a hot key expires and serving confidently wrong stale data. Keep this concrete and numeric — the arithmetic is the point.

cards.title: Effective latency is dominated by the miss path, not the hit path
cards.summary: A 90% hit rate isn't twice as good as 80% — the math says something much sharper.
cards.body:
A cache is a bet that the same data will be requested again soon. The payoff of that bet is computable: `effective_latency = hit_rate * fast_path + (1 - hit_rate) * slow_path`.

Say the fast path (cache hit) is 1ms and the slow path (cache miss, hit the database) is 100ms. At an 80% hit rate: `0.8 * 1 + 0.2 * 100 = 20.8ms`. At a 90% hit rate: `0.9 * 1 + 0.1 * 100 = 10.9ms`. Going from 80% to 90% — a ten-point improvement — very nearly *halved* the effective latency, because the miss term is a hundred times more expensive than the hit term and it's the miss term that dominates the whole equation.

This is the arithmetic reason cache design obsesses over the miss path and over squeezing the last few points of hit rate: the value of hit rate is wildly non-linear, and most of the real cost sits in the tail you're missing on.

cards.title: A cold cache is a temporary version of having no cache at all
cards.summary: Deploys and restarts reset your hit rate to zero, and the arithmetic still applies.
cards.body:
The hit-rate arithmetic doesn't care why the hit rate is low — only that it is. A freshly deployed cache instance, or one that just failed over, starts completely empty: every single request is a miss until enough traffic has passed through to warm it back up. During that window, the system is effectively paying the full slow-path cost on every request, exactly as if the cache didn't exist.

For a cache serving significant traffic, a cold start can look like a mini-outage — the database suddenly sees load it hasn't seen in a while, right when the cache infrastructure was already the thing that just changed. Strategies like pre-warming (populating known-hot keys before cutting over traffic) or restoring from a snapshot exist specifically to avoid paying that full re-warm cost at the worst possible moment.

cards.title: A TTL is a bet on how long staleness is tolerable, not a correctness guarantee
cards.summary: Every cached value with an expiry is, for some window, allowed to be wrong.
cards.body:
Setting a TTL (time-to-live) on a cached value is an explicit statement: 'I am willing to serve data that is up to this many seconds old.' That's a legitimate tradeoff — it avoids the cost and complexity of tracking every place a value needs to be invalidated — but it means the cache is, by design, sometimes lying, and the TTL is the bound on how badly.

A short TTL keeps staleness tight but pushes more traffic to the slow path and back toward the arithmetic where hit rate dominates cost. A long TTL protects hit rate but widens the staleness window — fine for a product description, much less fine for an account balance.

Explicit invalidation (actively clearing a key the moment its underlying data changes) is more correct than a TTL, but it's genuinely harder: it requires every write path to know what it's invalidating, and it's easy to miss a code path and leave a value stale indefinitely. Most real systems use both — TTLs as a safety net, invalidation where it's tractable.

cards.title: Cache-aside and write-through disagree about who fills the cache, and when
cards.summary: One caches lazily on read; the other keeps the cache warm on every write.
cards.body:
```diagram
Cache-aside:
read --> cache miss --> read DB --> write to cache --> return
write --> write DB only (cache goes stale or is invalidated)

Write-through:
write --> write cache AND DB together --> return
read --> cache is already warm --> return from cache
```

Cache-aside populates the cache reactively, on the read path, after a miss. **Write-through** populates it proactively, on the write path, so a value is in the cache before anyone has asked for it — every write updates both the cache and the database as one step.

Write-through trades a slightly slower write (you're now writing to two places) for reads that are much less likely to miss, since data is cached the moment it's created rather than the moment it's first requested. It's the right shape when you know written data will be read again soon; cache-aside is the right shape when most written data is never read again and you don't want to pay to cache it speculatively.

cards.title: Cache-aside: the application, not the cache, owns the miss
cards.summary: The most common caching pattern is just three lines around the read path.
cards.body:
```python
def get_user(user_id):
    cached = redis.get(f"user:{user_id}")
    if cached is not None:
        return json.loads(cached)

    user = db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s", user_id)
    redis.setex(f"user:{user_id}", 300, json.dumps(user))  # TTL: 300s
    return user
```

This is **cache-aside** (also called lazy loading): the application checks the cache first, and only on a miss does it go to the database — then it populates the cache itself for next time. It's the default pattern because it's simple, it only caches things that are actually requested, and a cache outage degrades gracefully to 'every request hits the database,' which is slow but not broken.

The cost is that the first request for any given key always pays the full miss latency, and the cache and database can drift out of sync if the write path doesn't also update or invalidate the cached value.

cards.title: Different cache layers hold different shapes of thing
cards.summary: 'Add a cache' is ambiguous until you say which layer and what it's caching.
cards.body:
A **browser cache** holds whole HTTP responses — static assets, sometimes full pages — right on the user's device, so a repeat visit doesn't even need a network round trip. A **CDN** holds the same kind of thing, but shared across many users at an edge location close to them, useful for anything not personalized.

An **application-level cache** (Redis, Memcached) typically holds smaller, structured values — a user record, a computed result, a session — things your own code reads and writes explicitly. A database's own **buffer pool** caches raw disk pages in memory so repeat reads of the same rows don't hit disk, invisibly to the application.

Each layer sits at a different point in the request chain and caches a different granularity of thing. A request can hit several of them in sequence, each one shaving off latency before the request ever reaches the next slower hop.

cards.title: Invalidation isn't just deleting a key — deleting a hot key can start a stampede
cards.summary: The moment you evict a popular key is exactly the moment demand for it doesn't stop.
cards.body:
❌ **Invalidation is just deleting the key** - the value changed, so you remove it from the cache and let the next reader repopulate it. Sounds complete.

✅ **Deleting a hot key can trigger a thundering herd** - if that key was being read a thousand times a second, the instant it's deleted, all thousand of those next requests miss simultaneously and hammer the database at once trying to refill the same value — a load spike the cache existed specifically to prevent. The fix isn't skipping invalidation; it's protecting the refill: a short lock or 'only one request refills, others wait' pattern, staggered/jittered TTLs so keys don't all expire in sync, or serving slightly stale data for a few hundred milliseconds while one request does the real work.

cards.title: Write-behind trades durability risk for write speed
cards.summary: Acknowledging a write before it's on disk is fast — until the cache disappears.
cards.body:
**Write-behind** (or write-back) caching acknowledges a write as soon as it hits the cache, then flushes it to the database asynchronously in the background rather than waiting for the database write to complete. Writes feel very fast because the caller never waits on the slow storage layer.

The cost is a durability window: if the cache crashes or the process dies before the flush happens, that write is gone, and the caller has no way to know — it was already told the write succeeded. This makes write-behind a reasonable choice for data where losing the last few seconds is tolerable (metrics, counters, ephemeral state) and a dangerous choice for anything where 'I told you it was saved' has to actually be true.

subtopics.title: Where the data lives: indexes, replicas, and the read path
subtopics.description: The database is usually the first thing to become the bottleneck, so a beginner needs a working model of why. Cover what an index actually is (a sorted structure that turns a scan into a lookup) and what it costs — every index is extra work on every write and extra disk. Cover why a query can ignore your index (wrong column order, function applied to the column, low selectivity) and how EXPLAIN is the tool that ends the guessing. Then cover replication as the first real scaling move: a primary takes writes, replicas serve reads, replication is asynchronous by default, and therefore a user can write a row and immediately not see it — read-your-writes is a real bug class, not a theoretical one. Finish with connection pooling and why a database dies of too many connections long before it dies of too much data.

cards.title: An index trades write cost and storage for read speed
cards.summary: An index is not free tuning — it's a resource you're spending on purpose.
cards.body:
An index is a separate, sorted structure that lets a database turn a full table scan (check every row) into a direct lookup (jump straight to the matching rows). That's why `WHERE email = ?` on an indexed column can be near-instant on a million-row table while the same lookup on an unindexed column scans the whole thing.

That speed isn't free. Every index has to be updated on every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` that touches the indexed column, which means more write work and more disk space, permanently, in exchange for faster reads on that column. A table with ten indexes doesn't just cost ten times the storage — every single write now updates ten data structures instead of one.

This is the same shape of trade you'll see again with replicas and connection pools throughout this subtopic: spend one resource (write throughput, storage, connections) to relieve pressure on another (read latency). Indexing isn't a free win you forgot to apply — it's a decision you're making about where the cost should live.

cards.title: A database dies of too many connections long before it dies of too much data
cards.summary: Each open connection holds real memory and a process/thread, whether it's doing anything or not.
cards.body:
Every open connection to a database costs real resources on the database side — typically a dedicated process or thread, plus memory for its session state — independent of whether that connection is actively running a query. It's common for a naive application to open a new database connection per request, which works fine at low traffic and then falls over hard the moment concurrent request volume approaches the database's connection limit, often in the low thousands or even hundreds depending on the engine and hardware.

A **connection pool** sits between the application and the database, maintaining a fixed, modest number of long-lived connections that requests borrow and return rather than opening fresh each time. This keeps the database's connection count bounded and predictable regardless of how many requests are in flight, which matters because a database exhausting its connection slots fails in an ugly, cascading way — new connection attempts start timing out or erroring, often well before the actual data workload was anywhere near a real limit.

cards.title: A full table scan isn't always the enemy
cards.summary: Sometimes reading everything is genuinely the fastest plan.
cards.body:
It's tempting to treat 'sequential scan' in an `EXPLAIN` output as a red flag that always means 'missing index.' That's not universally true. If a query is going to return a large fraction of the table's rows anyway — say, more than 10-20% — reading the table sequentially, in physical disk order, can be faster than the random-access jumping an index would require to fetch the same rows scattered across the table.

This is also why small tables are frequently scanned in full even with an index available: for a table with a few hundred rows, the overhead of consulting an index structure isn't worth the savings, and the planner correctly figures that out. The instinct to add an index the moment you see a scan is worth resisting until you've checked whether the query's own selectivity would have made the index worthwhile in the first place.

cards.title: A primary takes writes; replicas exist to absorb reads
cards.summary: Replication is the first scaling move most systems reach for, and it only scales one side.
cards.body:
```diagram
writes --> primary
              | (replication stream, asynchronous)
              +---------------> replica 1  <-- reads
              +- - - lag - - -> replica 2  <-- reads
```

Once a single database is under read pressure, the standard first move is **read replicas**: copies of the primary that continuously receive its changes and can serve read queries independently. The application routes writes to the primary and spreads reads across replicas, multiplying read capacity without touching write capacity at all.

The dashed arrow matters: replication is asynchronous by default, meaning a replica is always slightly behind the primary. Write capacity doesn't scale this way — every replica still has to receive and apply every write eventually, so this move relieves read load, not write load, and it introduces a new variable (lag) that didn't exist with a single database.

cards.title: Column order in a composite index is not a formality
cards.summary: An index on (a, b) is not the same index as one on (b, a).
cards.body:
A composite index is a single sorted structure over multiple columns, sorted by the first column, then the second within each value of the first, and so on — like a phone book sorted by last name, then first name. That means an index on `(user_id, created_at)` can efficiently serve `WHERE user_id = ?` and `WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at > ?`, because both queries can walk the sorted structure directly.

The same index is close to useless for `WHERE created_at > ?` alone, because `created_at` values for different users are scattered throughout the index, not grouped together — there's no contiguous range to jump to. The general rule: put the column used for equality filtering first, and the column used for sorting or range filtering after it, matching how the queries that need to be fast actually filter and sort.

cards.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE ends the guessing about what a query actually does
cards.summary: Stop assuming an index is being used — ask the database directly.
cards.body:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created ON orders (user_id, created_at);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

`EXPLAIN` shows the query planner's chosen execution plan — whether it's using an index scan or falling back to a sequential scan, and in what order it's joining tables. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually runs the query and reports real timings and row counts alongside the plan, so you can see not just what the planner intended but what actually happened.

A composite index like the one above, on `(user_id, created_at)`, is built specifically to serve this query: filter by `user_id`, then return rows already sorted by `created_at`. Guessing whether an index is helping is unnecessary when the tool that tells you for certain is one command away.

cards.title: Low selectivity means an index can cost more than it saves
cards.summary: An index on a column with only two values is often worse than no index at all.
cards.body:
An index earns its keep by letting the database skip most of the rows in a table. That only works well when the indexed value is **selective** — when matching it narrows the result down to a small fraction of the table. A `user_id` column, where each value matches a handful of rows out of millions, is highly selective and a great index candidate.

A `status` column with three possible values (`active`, `pending`, `deleted`), where each value matches a third of the table, is not. Using the index to fetch a third of a table's rows one at a time, jumping around the disk, is often slower than just scanning the table sequentially — so the planner will often correctly ignore a low-selectivity index in favor of a full scan, which can be confusing if you assumed the index was 'supposed' to help.

cards.title: Read replicas don't just make reads faster — they make some reads wrong
cards.summary: 'Add a replica' sounds like a pure win until a user can't see what they just wrote.
cards.body:
❌ **Read replicas make reads correct and faster** - more capacity to serve reads from, spread across more machines, sounds like an unambiguous improvement with no downside.

✅ **Replication lag breaks read-your-writes** - because replication is asynchronous, a replica can lag behind the primary by anywhere from milliseconds to (under load) seconds. A user who just submitted a form, then gets routed to a lagging replica on the very next page load, can see their own change appear to not have happened. This is a real, common bug class — 'I saved it and it's gone' — not a theoretical edge case, and it's the direct cost of the read-scaling win, not a separate unrelated problem.

cards.title: Wrapping a column in a function makes its index invisible
cards.summary: An index on `email` does nothing for a query that searches on `lower(email)`.
cards.body:
```sql
-- Index exists on email, but this query can't use it:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'jane@example.com';

-- Fix: index the expression itself
CREATE INDEX idx_users_lower_email ON users (lower(email));
-- now the original query can use it
```

A standard index is built on the literal stored value of a column. The moment a query applies a function to that column before comparing it — `lower()`, `date()`, string concatenation, anything — the database can no longer match rows against the index directly, because the index doesn't contain lowercased emails, it contains the emails as stored. It falls back to scanning every row and applying the function to each one.

This is one of the most common reasons a query 'has an index but is still slow.' The fix is either to index the expression itself (as above), to normalize the data at write time so no function is needed at query time, or to rewrite the query to compare against the raw column.

subtopics.title: Consistency models and the tradeoff CAP actually names
subtopics.description: Consistency is not one thing, it is a menu, and most production arguments are people using the word for different items on it. Teach the ladder concretely: strong/linearizable, sequential, causal, read-your-writes and monotonic-reads session guarantees, and eventual — with a user-visible symptom for each level, not just a definition. Correct the popular misreading of CAP: the choice is not 'pick two', it is 'during a network partition, do you refuse the request or answer possibly-stale', and outside a partition you are choosing between latency and consistency (the PACELC framing). Cover quorum arithmetic (R + W > N) as the tunable dial that makes this concrete, and why 'eventually consistent' says nothing about how long eventually is. Also cover the ACID transaction's isolation levels as the single-node cousin of this same ladder, so read-committed vs repeatable-read vs serializable is not a separate mystery.

cards.title: Consistency is a spectrum you choose per operation, not per system
cards.summary: A single well-designed system routinely runs at several consistency levels at once.
cards.body:
'Consistency' gets used as if it were one setting, but it's really a ladder of guarantees, each with a user-visible symptom:

- **Strong (linearizable)**: every read sees the latest write, as if there were only one copy of the data. A payment balance needs this.
- **Causal**: operations that are causally related (a reply to a comment) are seen in the right order by everyone, though unrelated operations can appear in any order.
- **Read-your-writes / monotonic-reads**: a specific user always sees their own recent writes and never sees time move backward, even if other users might momentarily see something older.
- **Eventual**: given no new writes, all replicas will *eventually* converge — with no promise about how long that takes.

The key move is realizing you don't pick one level for your whole system — you pick a level per operation, priced against latency and availability. A payment write might run at strong consistency while a 'likes' counter on the same page runs eventually consistent, because being briefly wrong about a like count costs nothing and being briefly wrong about a balance costs a lot. Every other idea in this subtopic — CAP, quorums, isolation levels — is really about how you buy a given point on this ladder.

cards.title: A dial you rarely see: consistency can differ by field, not just by table
cards.summary: Two columns in the same row can legitimately live at different points on the ladder.
cards.body:
It's natural to think of a consistency level as something you set for a table, a service, or a whole database. In practice, the more precise unit is often the individual field or operation. A social post's `text` and `author_id` might be written with strong consistency — you never want two authors attached to one post. Its `like_count`, updated thousands of times a second, might be maintained as an eventually-consistent counter that occasionally under- or over-counts by a small margin before converging.

Treating consistency as a per-field decision, rather than an all-or-nothing property of a system, is usually what lets a design hit both its correctness requirements and its performance targets — paying the coordination cost only where being wrong is actually expensive.

cards.title: CAP doesn't offer you a choice of two out of three
cards.summary: Partitions aren't optional, so 'pick two' was never really the theorem's claim.
cards.body:
❌ **CAP says you pick two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance** - so a team says 'we're a CP system' or 'we're AP' as if partition tolerance were an ingredient you could leave out of the recipe, like choosing not to worry about network splits.

✅ **A network partition will happen whether you plan for it or not, so the real choice is C or A while it's happening** - partition tolerance isn't a third option to trade away, because you don't get a vote on whether the network partitions. The actual decision CAP forces is: when a partition occurs and a node can't reach the rest of the cluster, does it refuse to answer (favoring consistency) or does it answer anyway with data that might be stale (favoring availability)? Outside of an active partition — which is most of the time — you're not choosing C vs A at all; you're trading latency against consistency, which is the PACELC extension of the same idea.

cards.title: Causal consistency preserves order without demanding a single global one
cards.summary: A reply appearing before the comment it replies to is the bug this guarantee prevents.
cards.body:
Strong consistency demands a single global order for every operation, everywhere — expensive. Eventual consistency demands no order at all — cheap but can produce visibly wrong results, like a reply to a comment appearing on someone's feed before the comment itself.

**Causal consistency** sits between them: it only guarantees ordering between operations that are actually causally related — if writing B happened after reading A, then anyone who sees B must also see A first. Two writes with no causal relationship (a stranger's unrelated post, made around the same time) can still appear in any order for different readers, and that's fine, because nothing about them was dependent on the other.

This is often enough to eliminate the specific ordering bugs that make eventual consistency feel broken to users, without paying the coordination cost of a total global order.

cards.title: During a partition, a node answers or it doesn't — that's the whole choice
cards.summary: Picture the split and the two possible responses become concrete.
cards.body:
```diagram
write --> Node A [value = 5]

            X   <-- network partition, A and B cannot talk

read  --> Node B [value = 3, stale]

Choice at Node B during the partition:
  CP: refuse the read (return an error) until it can confirm it's current
  AP: answer with 3 anyway, clearly marked or not, and let it be stale
```

With the partition drawn out, the abstract 'C or A' choice becomes a concrete decision one node has to make in the moment: a client is asking it for a value, it cannot currently confirm that value is up to date, and it has to either refuse (an error, or a redirect to try elsewhere) or answer with what it has. Every partition-tolerant system is implicitly making this choice somewhere, even if nobody wrote it down as a CAP tradeoff.

cards.title: 'Eventually' consistent says nothing about how long eventually takes
cards.summary: The word promises convergence, not a deadline.
cards.body:
Eventual consistency guarantees that if writes stop, all replicas will converge to the same value — eventually. What it deliberately does not specify is any bound on that window. In a healthy, low-latency system, convergence might happen in milliseconds and be practically invisible. Under load, network issues, or a struggling replica, that window can stretch to seconds or, in pathological cases, much longer.

This matters because 'eventually consistent' is often used reassuringly, as if it were a soft form of correctness. It's more accurate to treat it as a guarantee with an unspecified timeout: fine for data where staleness of unknown duration is truly tolerable, and risky to rely on wherever a user or another system needs to know *when* they can trust what they're reading, not just that they eventually will be able to.

cards.title: Isolation levels are the same ladder, scoped to a single node
cards.summary: Read-committed, repeatable-read, and serializable are consistency tradeoffs you're already used to.
cards.body:
```sql
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
-- sees any row that has been committed by other transactions,
-- even if that changes between two reads in this same transaction

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
-- guarantees the same query returns the same rows for the
-- whole transaction, no matter what else commits meanwhile

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- behaves as if transactions ran one at a time, in some order
```

These aren't a separate topic from the distributed consistency ladder — they're its single-node cousin. **Read committed** is the loosest and fastest: you might see different results from the same query run twice in one transaction, because other committed writes are visible in between. **Repeatable read** locks in a consistent snapshot for the transaction's duration. **Serializable** is the strongest: transactions behave as if fully ordered, at the cost of more locking or more aborted-and-retried transactions under contention.

The same principle applies: stronger isolation costs throughput and concurrency, and the right level is chosen per transaction based on what it can't afford to get wrong — exactly like choosing a point on the distributed consistency spectrum.

cards.title: Quorums are the dial that makes the consistency-availability tradeoff literal
cards.summary: R + W > N is a formula, not folklore.
cards.body:
In a system that replicates data across N nodes, a **write quorum** (W) is how many nodes must acknowledge a write before it's considered successful, and a **read quorum** (R) is how many nodes must respond before a read is returned. The rule `R + W > N` guarantees that any read quorum and any write quorum overlap on at least one node — so a read is guaranteed to see the most recent write, giving you strong consistency.

With N=3, setting W=2 and R=2 satisfies `R + W > N` (4 > 3): every write needs two of three nodes to confirm, every read checks two of three nodes, and those two sets must share at least one node that has the latest value. Lower W to 1 and writes get faster and more available, but R + W no longer exceeds N, so a read might land entirely on nodes that haven't seen the latest write yet — you've traded consistency for write latency and availability, and you can see exactly how much by the arithmetic.

cards.title: Session guarantees fix the specific bugs users actually notice
cards.summary: Read-your-writes and monotonic-reads are narrower promises than 'strong consistency,' and cheaper to buy.
cards.body:
Full strong consistency is expensive to offer everywhere, but most of the user-visible weirdness that eventual consistency causes comes from a much narrower set of problems, which is why session-scoped guarantees exist as a cheaper middle ground.

**Read-your-writes** guarantees that a specific user, in their own session, always sees writes they themselves just made — even if other users might not see that write yet. **Monotonic reads** guarantees that a user's successive reads never go backward in time, even if they hit different, differently-lagged replicas.

Both can often be implemented cheaply — routing a user's reads to the primary (or a replica known to be caught up) for a short window after they write, or pinning a session to one replica for its duration — without paying for global strong consistency across every user and every replica.

subtopics.title: Queues, async work, and the guarantees you really get
subtopics.description: Moving work off the request path is the highest-leverage architectural move available, and it changes the failure model rather than removing failure. Cover why you queue (smoothing bursts, decoupling producer from consumer lifetime, retrying without holding a user's connection) and what you give up (end-to-end visibility, ordering, immediate error reporting). Then get precise about delivery: at-most-once, at-least-once, and why exactly-once delivery does not exist on the wire — what real systems provide is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, which is exactly-once effect. Cover idempotency keys as the concrete implementation of that, ordering guarantees being per-partition and not global, consumer lag as the metric that tells you the truth about a queue's health, and dead-letter queues as the place poison messages go so one bad message cannot stall a partition forever.

cards.title: Exactly-once delivery doesn't exist — exactly-once effect does
cards.summary: The wire will duplicate messages; idempotent processing is how you make that harmless.
cards.body:
It's a persistent myth that a sufficiently good message queue can guarantee **exactly-once delivery** — that every message arrives at the consumer precisely one time, no more, no less. It can't, not durably, because the network between producer, broker, and consumer can always fail at exactly the wrong moment: a consumer can process a message and crash before it acknowledges receipt, and when it comes back, the broker (having never gotten the ack) redelivers a message that was already handled.

What real systems provide instead is **at-least-once delivery**: a message is guaranteed to arrive one or more times, never zero. The way you get the *effect* of exactly-once is by making the consumer's processing **idempotent** — safe to apply the same message twice with no difference in outcome. At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer equals exactly-once effect, and that combination, not a delivery guarantee alone, is the actual working pattern every reliable async system relies on.

cards.title: An idempotency key turns a duplicate message into a no-op
cards.summary: The database itself can be the thing that enforces 'already processed.'
cards.body:
```sql
-- idempotency_key is a UNIQUE column on the table
INSERT INTO processed_orders (idempotency_key, order_id, amount)
VALUES ('evt_8f2a91', 'ord_1123', 4999)
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING;
```

The consumer attaches a unique key to each unit of work — often generated by the producer and carried along with the message — and records it as part of the same transaction that does the real work. If the message is redelivered and the consumer tries to process it again, the `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` (or the equivalent unique-constraint violation) means the second attempt simply does nothing instead of double-charging a card or double-sending an email.

The same pattern works with a Redis guard: `SET key NX EX 3600` succeeds only if the key doesn't already exist, giving a cheap, time-bounded 'have I seen this before' check without a full database round trip.

cards.title: A poison message shouldn't be able to stall an entire partition
cards.summary: Dead-letter queues exist so one bad message doesn't block everything behind it.
cards.body:
```diagram
producer --> queue (partitioned) --> consumer group
                                          |
                                          +--> (fails repeatedly) --> dead-letter queue
```

If a consumer retries a message that fails every time — malformed data, a bug triggered by this specific payload, a dependency that's permanently unreachable for this input — and the queue keeps redelivering it at the front of the line, that one message can block every message behind it in the same partition, potentially forever.

A **dead-letter queue** is the escape valve: after a bounded number of failed attempts, the message is moved out of the main queue into a separate holding queue for inspection, and processing of the main partition continues. It converts an unbounded stall into a bounded number of retries plus a manageable, inspectable backlog of the messages that genuinely couldn't be processed.

cards.title: Async work changes the failure model — it doesn't remove failure
cards.summary: You trade 'the user sees an error immediately' for 'something is wrong somewhere and no one's watching yet.'
cards.body:
Moving work off the request path genuinely helps with bursts (a queue smooths a spike into a steadier processing rate) and with decoupling lifetimes, but it isn't a way to make failure go away — it changes what failure looks like. A synchronous call that fails produces an immediate error the caller can see and react to right then. An async job that fails happens somewhere off-screen, with no one watching in real time, and 'immediate error reporting' becomes 'someone eventually notices the dead-letter queue has messages in it, or a dashboard shows rising lag.'

This is a real cost, not a footnote: async systems need their own observability — metrics on lag, failure rate, and retry counts — because the ordinary signal a synchronous caller gets for free (an exception, a non-200 response) simply isn't there anymore.

cards.title: Consumer lag is the metric that tells you the truth about a queue's health
cards.summary: A queue that looks calm from the outside can be quietly falling behind.
cards.body:
**Consumer lag** is the gap between the newest message produced and the newest message a consumer has actually processed — how far behind the consumer is. It's the single most honest health signal for an async pipeline, because a queue itself can look perfectly healthy (accepting writes, no errors) while its consumers slowly fall further and further behind.

Growing lag means one of two things: consumers aren't fast enough for the current production rate, or something is actively broken (a crash-looping consumer, a downstream dependency it's blocked on). Either way, lag is a leading indicator — by the time it shows up as a user-visible symptom (a delayed email, a stale feed), the backlog has often already been building for a while. Alerting on lag directly, rather than on downstream symptoms, is what catches the problem while it's still small.

cards.title: Queue ordering holds within a partition, not across the whole topic
cards.summary: 'The queue preserves order' is only ever locally true.
cards.body:
A common assumption is that a message queue delivers messages in the exact order they were produced, globally. That's not what most queues that support any horizontal scaling actually offer, because a queue that serialized everything through one ordered stream couldn't be parallelized.

What's typically guaranteed is ordering **within a partition** — a queue is split into multiple partitions (often keyed by something like a user ID or entity ID), and only messages within the same partition are guaranteed to arrive in the order they were sent. Two messages in different partitions can be delivered, processed, and completed in any relative order, including 'out of order' from a global perspective.

This is usually fine, because the ordering guarantee you actually need is almost always scoped the same way — 'events for this one user arrive in order' — not 'every event across the entire system arrives in global order,' which would be far more expensive to provide and rarely what the business logic even requires.

cards.title: Queuing decouples a producer's lifetime from its consumer's
cards.summary: The caller doesn't have to be alive, connected, or waiting for the work to eventually happen.
cards.body:
A synchronous call requires both sides to be up and connected for the duration of the work. Putting a queue between a producer and a consumer breaks that requirement: the producer can enqueue a message and move on immediately, and the consumer can process it seconds, minutes, or — if it's down and later recovers — hours later, without the producer needing to still be around or even care.

This is the core reason queuing is the highest-leverage move available for moving work off a request's critical path: sending a welcome email, generating a report, resizing an uploaded image — none of these need to happen before the user's request returns, and forcing them onto the request path just adds their full latency (and their full chance of failure) to something the user is actively waiting on.

cards.title: Retries only belong on operations that can safely be repeated
cards.summary: An idempotent write can be retried freely; a 'charge the card' call cannot, without protection.
cards.body:
A queue consumer that fails processing a message will typically retry it — that's part of what makes at-least-once delivery useful rather than fragile. But retrying is only safe if the operation being retried is **idempotent**: running it twice produces the same end state as running it once.

An operation like 'set the user's status to active' is naturally idempotent — repeating it changes nothing the second time. An operation like 'charge this card $50' or 'increment the counter by 1' is not — repeating it blindly causes real, user-visible harm (a double charge, an inflated count). This is exactly why idempotency keys matter: they're what turns a naturally non-idempotent operation into a safely retryable one, by giving the consumer a way to recognize 'I've already done this' before doing it again.

cards.title: 'We need exactly-once delivery' is usually solving the wrong layer
cards.summary: The guarantee you actually need lives in the consumer, not the transport.
cards.body:
❌ **We need exactly-once delivery from the queue** - teams sometimes spend real effort evaluating message brokers specifically for an exactly-once delivery claim, treating it as a property the transport layer should provide so the application doesn't have to think about duplicates.

✅ **At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer gives you the same outcome, reliably** - no broker can eliminate the network failure modes that cause redelivery, so any broker claiming true exactly-once is either narrowly scoping the guarantee (e.g. only within its own internal pipeline, not end-to-end to your consumer) or quietly relying on idempotency underneath. Building idempotent processing directly is more robust than trusting a transport-level promise, and it works with any broker, including the simplest ones.

subtopics.title: Partitioning and the shard key you cannot take back
subtopics.description: When one machine can no longer hold the data or the write load, you split it — and the choice of what to split on is the most expensive decision in the system because migrating a shard key means rewriting the data layout. Distinguish vertical partitioning (splitting tables/columns by concern) from horizontal sharding (splitting rows), and cover the three main routing strategies: range-based (great for range scans, prone to hotspots on sequential keys), hash-based (even spread, destroys range queries), and directory/lookup-based (flexible, adds a lookup hop and a component that must not go down). Teach consistent hashing as the fix for the resharding problem — why naive hash(key) % N reshuffles almost everything when N changes, and how a hash ring with virtual nodes moves only 1/N of the keys. Cover the hot partition / celebrity key problem and the queries that become expensive after sharding: cross-shard joins, global secondary indexes, and anything needing a total ordering.

cards.title: The shard key decides which queries stay cheap and which become distributed
cards.summary: Choose it from your access patterns, not from whatever looks like a natural ID.
cards.body:
Once a single database can no longer hold the data or the write load, the fix is to split it across multiple machines — **sharding**. The single most consequential decision in that process is the **shard key**: the value used to decide which shard a given row lives on.

Whichever queries filter or group by the shard key stay cheap — they can be routed to exactly the shard that holds the answer. Every other query — anything that needs to join across shards, aggregate globally, or sort by something other than the shard key — becomes expensive, because it now has to fan out to every shard and merge the results.

This is why the shard key is described as a decision you cannot easily take back: changing it later means physically re-migrating every row to a potentially different shard, often while the system stays live. Picking it correctly up front, based on how the data is actually queried rather than what looks like the obvious primary key, is the highest-leverage decision in the whole exercise — hotspots, cross-shard joins, and rebalancing pain are all downstream consequences of this one choice.

cards.title: Consistent hashing makes adding a node move only a fraction of the keys
cards.summary: A hash ring with virtual nodes fixes what modulo sharding gets wrong.
cards.body:
```diagram
        node A
      /        \
  node D        node B
      \        /
        node C

keys hash onto positions on the ring;
each key belongs to the next node clockwise.
Adding node E only steals the keys in the
arc between its position and the next node —
every other arc is untouched.
```

Consistent hashing places both shards and keys onto positions on a conceptual ring (via hashing), and each key belongs to whichever shard is next going clockwise. Adding a new shard only affects the keys that fall in the arc immediately preceding its new position — roughly `1/N` of all keys — leaving every other key's assignment untouched.

Real implementations use many **virtual nodes** per physical shard (each physical shard occupies dozens of positions on the ring) to keep the resulting distribution close to even, since a single point per shard can otherwise create an uneven split of the ring's arcs.

cards.title: Naive modulo sharding reshuffles almost everything when you add a node
cards.summary: hash(key) % N looks harmless until N changes.
cards.body:
```python
def shard_for(key, n):
    return hash(key) % n

keys = [f"user_{i}" for i in range(20)]
moved = sum(1 for k in keys if shard_for(k, 4) != shard_for(k, 5))
print(f"{moved}/{len(keys)} keys moved when going from 4 to 5 shards")
# typically prints something like: 16/20 keys moved
```

The naive approach — hash a key and take it modulo the number of shards — works fine as long as the number of shards never changes. The moment you add or remove a shard, `N` changes, and because modulo is sensitive to the exact value of `N`, the vast majority of keys land on a different shard than before, even though only one shard was added. In production terms, that means near-total data migration to add a single node — exactly the operation you'd want scaling to make *cheap*.

cards.title: Range, hash, and directory routing trade off differently
cards.summary: There's no universally best sharding strategy — only one best for your query pattern.
cards.body:
**Range-based** sharding assigns contiguous key ranges to shards (users A-F on shard 1, G-M on shard 2, and so on). It's excellent for range scans — 'give me everything between X and Y' stays on one or a few shards — but it's prone to hotspots when keys are written sequentially, like timestamps or auto-incrementing IDs, because all recent writes pile onto the same shard.

**Hash-based** sharding hashes the key before assigning it to a shard, which spreads writes evenly regardless of key pattern, but destroys range queries — 'everything between X and Y' is now scattered across every shard, since the hash has no relationship to the original ordering.

**Directory-based** (lookup) sharding keeps an explicit table mapping keys or key ranges to shards. It's the most flexible — you can rebalance by editing the mapping rather than rehashing everything — but it adds a lookup hop to every query, and that lookup service itself becomes a component that must never go down, since everything else depends on asking it where to go.

cards.title: Resharding live is one of the riskiest operations in a distributed system
cards.summary: Migrating a shard key means moving data while the system keeps serving traffic.
cards.body:
Because the shard key is so hard to change, teams that get it wrong (or simply outgrow the original choice) eventually face a live resharding: moving data to new shard boundaries while reads and writes keep happening. The dangerous part isn't the copy — it's staying correct during the window where some data has moved and some hasn't, and new writes have to be routed correctly to wherever the *current* authoritative copy lives.

Common approaches include dual-writing to both the old and new layout during a transition window, then cutting reads over once the new layout is verified caught up, or using a directory/lookup layer specifically so the shard assignment can change without every client needing to know about it. Whatever the mechanism, resharding is treated as a first-class, carefully staged migration project — not a config change — precisely because getting the shard key wrong the first time is expensive to undo.

cards.title: 'Shard by user_id, it's evenly distributed' ignores who your users actually are
cards.summary: Even key distribution doesn't protect you from one key getting all the traffic.
cards.body:
❌ **Shard by user_id — it's evenly distributed** - user IDs are effectively random or sequential, so hashing them spreads rows evenly across shards, and 'evenly distributed' sounds like the whole hotspot problem is solved.

✅ **A celebrity or hot-tenant key concentrates load regardless of how evenly keys are distributed** - even distribution of *rows* says nothing about even distribution of *traffic*. If one user is a celebrity account with a million followers generating constant reads, or one tenant in a multi-tenant system is far larger and more active than the rest, that single shard key routes a disproportionate share of *requests* — not rows — to one shard, and that shard becomes the bottleneck no matter how evenly the key space itself was hashed.

cards.title: Sharding turns some queries into cross-shard problems
cards.summary: A join or a global index that was one query becomes N queries plus a merge.
cards.body:
A query like `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42` shards cleanly if `user_id` is the shard key — it goes to exactly one shard. But a query like `SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.id WHERE p.category = 'electronics'`, where `products` might be sharded by `product_id` and unrelated to `user_id`, no longer has a single shard that can answer it — it becomes N separate queries, one per shard, followed by the application (or a query-federation layer) stitching the results back together.

The same problem hits any **global secondary index** — an index on a column other than the shard key, since matching rows can be scattered across every shard — and anything requiring a **total ordering** across the whole dataset, like 'the 10 most recent orders across all users,' which now requires querying every shard and merging by timestamp rather than a single ordered index lookup.

cards.title: Vertical partitioning splits by concern before horizontal sharding splits by row
cards.summary: Not every scaling problem needs multiple copies of the schema.
cards.body:
**Vertical partitioning** splits a single table (or database) by column or by feature area, rather than by row — user profile data in one database, billing data in another, activity logs in a third. It's often the first, cheapest move: it isolates load and failure by concern (a billing outage doesn't take down profile lookups) and it's a purely organizational change to the schema, not a new distributed-query problem.

**Horizontal sharding**, splitting rows of the *same* logical table across multiple machines, is the heavier move, reached for once a single table's row count or write volume genuinely outgrows one machine's capacity, regardless of how well-separated the schema already is. Vertical partitioning and horizontal sharding aren't competing options — they're often layered: split vertically by concern first, then shard horizontally within whichever concern actually needs it.

subtopics.title: Designing for failure: timeouts, retries, and backpressure
subtopics.description: In a distributed system, failure is an input to the design, not an exception path bolted on later. Start with the fact that every remote call needs a timeout and that an unbounded call is a resource leak waiting for traffic. Then the retry trap: naive retries turn a brief degradation into a self-sustaining outage, so retries need exponential backoff, jitter to break synchronization, a bounded budget, and must only be applied to idempotent operations. Cover the circuit breaker as the pattern that stops sending requests into a service that is already down, and its half-open state as the controlled way back. Cover backpressure and load shedding — a queue that grows without bound converts a throughput problem into a latency problem and then into a memory outage — and why shedding 5% of requests fast is better than serving 100% slowly. Include cascading failure and bulkheads: isolating resource pools so one slow dependency cannot consume every thread.

cards.title: Every remote call needs a deadline and a bounded retry budget
cards.summary: Unbounded waiting and unbounded retrying are the two ways one slow dependency becomes a full outage.
cards.body:
A remote call without a timeout is a resource leak waiting for the right kind of traffic: the thread, connection, or memory holding that call open never gets freed as long as the other side stays slow but not fully dead — which is often the worst-behaved state a dependency can be in, since 'obviously down' is easy to detect and route around, but 'technically responding, just very slowly' quietly ties up resources indefinitely.

The natural fix — retry on failure — introduces its own unbounded-exposure risk if left unconstrained. A retry without a cap, applied by every caller, of every request, against a dependency that's already struggling, doesn't help it recover; it adds load on top of the load that caused the trouble in the first place.

Every other pattern in this subtopic — circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding — is a refinement of the same underlying principle: bound how much you're willing to wait, and bound how much you're willing to retry, so that a single slow dependency has a hard ceiling on how much of your system it can drag down with it.

cards.title: A circuit breaker stops sending requests into a service that's already down
cards.summary: Closed, open, half-open: the state machine that governs when to give up trying and when to try again.
cards.body:
```diagram
closed --> (failure threshold exceeded) --> open
open --> (timeout elapses) --> half-open
half-open --> (test request succeeds) --> closed
half-open --> (test request fails) --> open
```

A circuit breaker sits in front of calls to a dependency and tracks its recent failure rate. In the **closed** state, requests flow through normally. Once failures cross a threshold, it trips to **open**: further requests fail immediately, locally, without even attempting the network call — sparing both the caller (no more waiting on timeouts) and the struggling dependency (no more load added to it while it's down).

After a cooldown period, the breaker moves to **half-open**: it lets a small number of test requests through to see if the dependency has recovered. If they succeed, it closes again and resumes normal traffic; if they fail, it reopens and waits longer. This is the controlled way back from 'stop calling it entirely' to 'trust it again,' without the abrupt full-traffic resumption that would just knock a barely-recovering service back down.

cards.title: An unbounded queue turns a throughput problem into a memory outage
cards.summary: A queue that grows without limit is not a safety buffer — it's a delayed and bigger failure.
cards.body:
When incoming work outpaces processing capacity, the instinctive fix is to queue the excess and work through it as capacity allows. That's fine as long as the queue has a bound. An **unbounded** queue accepts everything indefinitely, which converts what should have been an immediate, visible problem (requests failing fast because the system is overloaded) into a hidden one: memory quietly grows as the backlog builds, latency for anything still in the queue climbs steadily since it's now waiting behind a growing line, and eventually the process runs out of memory and crashes — taking down whatever *was* still being processed along with everything waiting.

A bounded queue with an explicit policy for what happens when it's full — reject new work, or shed the oldest/least important items — turns an eventual, catastrophic failure into an immediate, contained, and recoverable one.

cards.title: A slow database can become a full outage through pure feedback
cards.summary: Cascading failure is a loop, not a single point of breakage.
cards.body:
```diagram
slow database
     |
     v
app threads blocked waiting on DB --> thread pool exhausted
     |
     v
upstream callers time out --> upstream callers retry
     |
     v
even more load hits the app --> more threads blocked
     |
     +----------------- feeds back into the loop -----------------+
```

No single component in this chain is catastrophically broken on its own — the database is merely slow, not down. But each stage feeds the next: slowness ties up threads, tied-up threads make the app itself appear slow or unresponsive to its callers, those callers time out and retry, and the retries add exactly the kind of load the app can least afford right now. What started as one dependency having a bad moment becomes a full outage purely through this feedback loop, which is why the fix has to break the loop at multiple points — timeouts, bounded retries, and isolating resource pools — rather than trying to fix 'the database' alone.

cards.title: A timeout without a sensible value is barely better than none at all
cards.summary: The number you pick has to reflect what the caller can actually tolerate.
cards.body:
Setting a timeout is necessary but not sufficient — the value matters. A timeout set far too high (say, 60 seconds on a call that should normally return in 50ms) still lets a slow dependency tie up resources for a very long time before finally giving up, providing little real protection. A timeout set far too low starts failing perfectly healthy requests that simply landed on a slightly slower-than-usual response, turning normal variance into unnecessary errors.

A reasonable timeout is usually derived from the dependency's own observed latency distribution — something like the p99 or p999 latency under normal load, with margin — rather than picked arbitrarily. It's also worth setting timeouts at every hop in a chain with awareness of the hops above and below it: a timeout set to the same value at every layer of a call chain means an inner timeout firing can still leave an outer caller waiting needlessly, so budgets are often allocated so each layer's timeout leaves room for the layers below it to fail cleanly first.

cards.title: Backoff with jitter is a few lines of code that prevent synchronized retries
cards.summary: Without randomness, every caller retries in lockstep and re-creates the exact spike they were trying to avoid.
cards.body:
```python
import random

def backoff_delay(attempt, base=0.1, cap=10.0):
    exp = min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)
    return random.uniform(0, exp)

# attempt 0: up to 0.1s, attempt 1: up to 0.2s,
# attempt 4: up to 1.6s, capped at 10s eventually
```

Exponential backoff alone — doubling the wait after each failure — sounds sufficient, but if every caller experienced the same failure at roughly the same moment (a common case: they were all calling the same now-overloaded dependency), they'll all wait the same doubling sequence and all retry again at the same moment, recreating the exact synchronized spike that caused the problem.

**Jitter** — picking a random delay up to the exponential ceiling rather than the ceiling itself — spreads those retries out over time instead of clustering them, which is what actually gives the struggling dependency room to recover rather than getting hit by another synchronized wave.

cards.title: Bulkheads keep one slow dependency from consuming every thread
cards.summary: Isolating resource pools contains damage the way a ship's compartments contain flooding.
cards.body:
Named after the watertight compartments in a ship's hull that keep flooding in one section from sinking the whole vessel, a **bulkhead** in software isolates the resource pool (threads, connections, memory) used for calls to one dependency from the pool used for calls to another. Without this, a single shared thread pool serving calls to five different downstream services means one of those services becoming slow can exhaust the entire pool — and now calls to the other four healthy services can't get a thread either, even though nothing is actually wrong with them.

Giving each dependency its own bounded pool means the worst a single slow dependency can do is exhaust *its own* allocation, leaving the rest of the system's capacity untouched and able to keep serving everything else normally.

cards.title: 'Retries make the system more reliable' is only true if they're bounded
cards.summary: An unbounded retry policy can multiply load onto a dependency that's already failing.
cards.body:
❌ **Retries make the system more reliable** - if a call fails, try again; that seems like straightforward defense against transient blips, and more retrying sounds strictly safer than less.

✅ **Naive retries amplify load on an already-struggling dependency** - if a service starts failing 20% of requests because it's overloaded, and every caller immediately retries every failure, the retried requests land right back on the same overloaded service, on top of new traffic still arriving — turning a 20% failure rate into a feedback loop that can push it toward 100%. The fix isn't 'don't retry' — it's **exponential backoff** (wait longer between each attempt), **jitter** (randomize the wait so retries from many callers don't all land at once), and a **bounded budget** (give up after N attempts) — and retries should only ever be applied to genuinely idempotent operations, so a retried request doesn't double the effect as well as the load.

cards.title: Shedding 5% of requests fast beats serving 100% slowly
cards.summary: Backpressure means choosing, on purpose, what gets dropped.
cards.body:
