cards.summary: Confidence and correctness are separate properties of a plan.
cards.body:
A plan built on one bad early assumption doesn't look shaky from the inside — every subsequent step follows logically from the one before it, and the whole thing reads as a competent, well-reasoned strategy. The flaw isn't in the reasoning chain, it's in the premise the chain started from.

This is what makes these failures harder to spot than an obviously broken plan: nothing about the execution signals a problem, because the execution genuinely is sound given the premise. Catching this requires checking the premise itself against reality — does the bug actually live where the plan assumes it does — not just checking whether each step logically follows the last.

cards.title: A fix that grows into a refactor nobody asked for
cards.summary: Each individual step looked reasonable; the sum wasn't what was requested.
cards.body:
Over-eager scope expansion rarely happens as one big leap — it happens as a series of locally reasonable extensions. Fixing a bug reveals an adjacent thing that looks messy; cleaning that up reveals another; by the end, the diff touches three times the surface area the original task described, and each individual step was defensible on its own terms.

The remedy is the same decomposition discipline as everywhere else in this subtopic: a task scoped to a checkable goal has a natural edge, and noticing when a step falls outside that edge — even a genuinely good idea — is a checkpoint worth having, whether it's the agent flagging it or a human reviewing the diff.

cards.title: Commit at each stage so recovery means resetting one, not abandoning the hour
cards.summary: A checkpoint is only useful if it's cheap to return to.
cards.body:
```bash
git add -A && git commit -m 'checkpoint: parser passes'
```

A commit at each verified stage turns 'this went wrong somewhere in the last hour' into 'this went wrong somewhere after this specific, known-good point.' Recovery becomes resetting to the last checkpoint and re-doing one stage, not discarding everything and starting over — which is the entire practical payoff of decomposition, made concrete.

cards.title: 'Done' asserted is not the same as 'done' verified
cards.summary: A confident report and a passing check are different kinds of evidence.
cards.body:
An agent can report a task complete because its internal model of the situation says the goal is met — without that belief having been checked against an actual run, test, or observable state. This is premature declaration of success: the words 'this is done' appearing in the transcript before anything confirmed it.

The fix isn't distrust of the agent's reports generally — it's insisting that a 'done' claim be paired with the evidence that earned it: the test output, the command's exit code, the diff. A report with no evidence attached is a claim, not a result, regardless of how confidently it's phrased.

cards.title: Draw the wrong turn and the checkpoints that would have caught it
cards.summary: An early mistake left unchecked shapes everything after it.
cards.body:
```diagram
turn 3: wrong assumption introduced
   |
   v
turn 8 --> turn 15 --> turn 22 --> turn 30  (all built on the assumption)
   ^           ^           ^           ^
   |           |           |           |
checkpoint  checkpoint  checkpoint  checkpoint
 (would    (would catch  (catches,   (never
  catch)    it later,     but 20     reached
            still cheap)  turns of   without
                          rework)    one)
```

Every checkpoint along this line is a chance to catch the same mistake at a different cost — cheapest right after it happens, most expensive the longer it's left running unexamined. A task with no checkpoints at all is the turn-30 outcome by default, not by bad luck.

cards.title: Drift is the agent's beliefs falling out of sync with reality
cards.summary: A lossy summary of turn five is still what turn fifty relies on.
cards.body:
As a session grows long, earlier context gets compacted into a summary — a real, useful mechanism, but a lossy one. Drift is what happens when the agent's later decisions are guided by that summary rather than the original detail, and the summary has quietly diverged from what actually happened.

It doesn't look like an obvious error in the moment — the agent is acting consistently with what it believes, it's just that what it believes has slipped. This is why tracing a drifted outcome usually means going back to find where the summary and the reality parted ways, not assuming the whole session's reasoning was unreliable throughout.

cards.title: The agent's report is a claim; the diff is the evidence
cards.summary: Check what changed, not just what was said about it.
cards.body:
❌ **The agent said the tests pass** - a clear, confident statement in the transcript, easy to take at face value.

✅ **That's a claim in the transcript; the run output and the diff are the evidence** - `git diff HEAD~1` shows exactly what changed in this stage, and the actual test output (not a paraphrase of it) shows exactly what ran and what it returned. A reviewer's job on agent-produced work is checking the claim against that evidence, the same skepticism applied to any report of work — agent-authored or not — that arrives without its receipts.
